title: Trump Claims U.S. Holds Iran War at “Status Quo,” Says American Troops “Locked and Loaded” – Live Updates
body:
President Donald Trump told CBS’s “60 Minutes” that the United States is deliberately maintaining a “status‑quo” stance in its confrontation with Iran, while simultaneously assuring that American forces are “locked and loaded” for any escalation. The remarks, delivered during a rare interview with the veteran news program, underscored the administration’s dual strategy of diplomatic restraint and military readiness, a posture that has drawn both praise and criticism from allies and regional observers.

Trump’s comments came as a senior United Arab Emirates official, Dr. Anwar Garg‑Gargash, warned that a decisive end to the U.S.–Iran conflict was unlikely for an extended period. Gargash, who serves as diplomatic adviser to the UAE president, said the war “will probably continue for a long time,” reflecting broader concerns in the Gulf that the rivalry between Washington and Tehran could destabilize the already volatile Middle East. The United Arab Emirates, a close U.S. partner, has been navigating a delicate balance between its economic ties with Iran and its security cooperation with Washington.

The president’s assertion that the war is a “good decision” in the long term—despite acknowledging short‑term hardships—appears rooted in a belief that sustained pressure will eventually force Tehran to curtail its regional ambitions and nuclear program. Critics argue that such a calculus overlooks the humanitarian toll on civilian populations and risks inflaming anti‑American sentiment across the Arab world. Moreover, policy analysts note that the United States has not formally declared war on Iran, making the terminology of “war” itself a point of contention. The ambiguous language allows the administration to justify a range of actions, from economic sanctions to limited kinetic strikes, without triggering the full legal and political ramifications of a declared war.

Military experts point to the “locked and loaded” remark as a signal to both allies and adversaries that U.S. forces remain on high alert. The Pentagon has recently increased the presence of carrier strike groups in the Persian Gulf and expanded joint exercises with regional partners, reinforcing deterrence. Yet, the same experts caution that overt displays of force can be a double‑edged sword, potentially provoking miscalculations. In past confrontations, such as the 2019 downing of a U.S. drone by Iran, the line between deterrence and escalation has proved thin.

International reaction to Trump’s statements has been mixed. European capitals, while supportive of a diplomatic solution, have urged Washington to avoid actions that could spiral into broader conflict. In Tehran, officials dismissed the U.S. leader’s comments as “bluster,” reiterating that Iran will defend its sovereignty and continue its “rightful” nuclear development. Meanwhile, Gulf Cooperation Council members, including Saudi Arabia and Qatar, have privately expressed unease about the prospect of a protracted standoff, fearing it could disrupt oil markets and exacerbate sectarian tensions.

Looking ahead, the trajectory of the U.S.–Iran confrontation will hinge on a complex interplay of diplomatic negotiations, economic pressures, and military posturing. If Washington can leverage its “status‑quo” approach to bring Iran back to the negotiating table, there may be a window for a renewed nuclear agreement and a de‑escalation of hostilities. Conversely, any misstep—whether a misinterpreted naval maneuver or an unintended strike—could ignite a wider regional conflict. As the world watches, the administration’s challenge will be to balance its promise of readiness with a credible pathway toward a sustainable, long‑term resolution.
